back: A clear, brief summary of the project's purpose: a realistic, attractive view of the future outcomes. It motivates and keeps people pulling in the same direction.

front: The four questions a vision should answer
back: What is the purpose? What defines successful work? How will the future be better? How will the team know it is drifting from the vision?
Sums up the project in a powerful phrase; describes the best achievable outcome; creates a common picture; inspires passion.
Team members and key stakeholders, collaboratively. A vision handed down is rarely shared.
A short, high-level description of what is expected of a product: target market, users, major benefits, what differentiates it.

front: First activity of leadership in the Eighth Edition
back: Establishing and maintaining vision.
The project vision or purpose, and a clear set of working agreements.
Why are we doing this? Who benefits and how? What does done mean (release criteria)? How will we work together?
The product manager or product owner, with its success metrics.
Purpose, then people, then process.
Communicate it throughout; refer to the intended outcomes when making decisions and solving problems; keep it visible.
The purpose of the project and its benefits held in common by the team; close to alignment with the organization's mission and strategy.
Review it regularly; rework it with stakeholders when the situation changes; then revisit the roadmap and backlog.
Joint vision workshop; one vision statement and roadmap for all teams; shared goal visible in release planning; every backlog item links to the vision.
A project brief or team charter stating the vision, mission and simple success tests; review the vision regularly.
Product vision, product roadmap, release plans, iterations, tasks.
Define the problem, identify the root cause, generate solutions, choose the best, implement, verify.
Finds the basic reason behind a problem; when all root causes are removed, the problem does not recur.
Keep asking why to get past the symptoms to the root cause.
Find out why: talk with those involved and define the problem before choosing a fix.

front: Facilitator's job in a vision workshop
back: Effective participation, mutual understanding, all contributions considered, buy-in under the agreed decision process, follow-up on agreements.
The vision summarizes the purpose; requirements state in detail what is needed.
Issued by the sponsor or initiator; tells the team why the project matters and where it is headed.

front: New team members and the vision
back: Cover the vision when bringing them in; the team charter is reviewed partly to orient new members.

front: Backlog item that does not serve the vision
back: Ask how it serves the vision; every backlog item should link back to it. The product owner decides on the backlog.
